title: Optimization & Constrained Problems
description: Study convexity and global optima, gradient descent and step size, lagrange multipliers and constraints, and stochastic gradients and variance. Each lesson includes a worked example and an applied practice task.

lessons.title: Convexity and global optima
lessons.description: State which guarantee transfers from the quadratic to the nonconvex case and which does not.
lessons.conceptOverview: For differentiable convex objectives, a zero gradient identifies a global minimum when it exists. Nonconvex objectives lack that guarantee, and strict convexity supports uniqueness under appropriate existence conditions.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: For differentiable convex objectives, a zero gradient identifies a global minimum when it exists. Nonconvex objectives lack that guarantee, and strict convexity supports uniqueness under appropriate existence conditions.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A convex quadratic has one minimum, while a neural-network objective may have many stationary points.

sections.title: Practice & verification
sections.content: State which guarantee transfers from the quadratic to the nonconvex case and which does not. Write down your reasoning and check it against the concept before continuing.

commonMistakes: Every zero gradient in a neural network is a unique global optimum.

lessons.title: Gradient descent and step size
lessons.description: Compare updates for alpha = 0.25 and alpha = 1.5.
lessons.conceptOverview: Gradient descent moves opposite the gradient with a chosen step size. Excessively large steps can oscillate or diverge even on a convex quadratic; progress depends on curvature and learning rate.
lessons.whyItMatters: A convex objective can still diverge under an unsuitable step size.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Gradient descent moves opposite the gradient with a chosen step size. Excessively large steps can oscillate or diverge even on a convex quadratic; progress depends on curvature and learning rate.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: For f(x) = x squared, the update is x next = (1 - 2 alpha)x. With alpha = 1.5 the magnitude doubles each step.

sections.title: Practice & verification
sections.content: Compare updates for alpha = 0.25 and alpha = 1.5. Write down your reasoning and check it against the concept before continuing.

keyTakeaways: A convex objective can still diverge under an unsuitable step size.
commonMistakes: Convexity makes every positive learning rate safe.

lessons.title: Lagrange multipliers and constraints
lessons.description: Solve the equality-constrained problem and verify feasibility.
lessons.conceptOverview: Lagrange multipliers combine an objective with equality constraints to derive stationary conditions. Inequality constraints require additional conditions such as complementary slackness; solving stationarity alone may produce infeasible candidates.
lessons.whyItMatters: Constrained candidates must satisfy both optimality conditions and constraints.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Lagrange multipliers combine an objective with equality constraints to derive stationary conditions. Inequality constraints require additional conditions such as complementary slackness; solving stationarity alone may produce infeasible candidates.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Minimizing x squared plus y squared subject to x + y = 1 yields equal coordinates at the optimum.

sections.title: Practice & verification
sections.content: Solve the equality-constrained problem and verify feasibility. Write down your reasoning and check it against the concept before continuing.

keyTakeaways: Constrained candidates must satisfy both optimality conditions and constraints.
commonMistakes: Any stationary point of the unconstrained objective solves the constrained problem.

lessons.title: Stochastic gradients and variance
lessons.description: Compare unbiased random sampling with the biased sampler.
lessons.conceptOverview: A stochastic gradient estimates the full-data gradient under sampling assumptions. Larger batches can reduce sampling variance but change compute cost and update frequency; biased sampling can invalidate the estimate.
lessons.whyItMatters: Sampling design affects whether a gradient estimates the intended objective.
